_doc: T-0581. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago: Munsell, 1895), read for what it says about the fifty lead surnames the Newberry genealogical index (T-0570) flagged against this work, and for what it says about the town those people lived in. THE VOLUME IS A COMPILER SIXTY YEARS AFTER THE FACT and cites Andreas, Bross and the Story of Chicago on the pages read here; every claim is transcription_mediated, none is scan_verified, and where the book credits another work in the sentence itself the claim says so. WHAT WAS READ AND WHAT WAS ONLY LOOKED UP is the distinction this file turns on: all forty-nine machine-readable lead surnames were searched across the whole 137,409-line text, and the mechanical result of that search is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json. Thirteen passages earned a claim. The rest are named in that file and in the source record's what_it_does_not_supply, because a surname that appears ninety-eight times in an index and a war chapter and never once in the town of 1835 is a finding too.
generated_by: hand — T-0581. The `quote` of every claim was filled programmatically from the committed text at its own locator so that no transcription step stands between the file and the gate; everything else in each claim is authored.

claims.normalized: Among those who came through Chicago in 1832 and decided to remain were Philo Carpenter and John S. Wright from Massachusetts; T. W. Goodrich, Hamilton Barnes and Dr. Philip Maxwell from New York; Dr. E. S. Kimberly and George W. Snow of Vermont; and Alanson Sweet.
claims.describes_date: 1832 — arrivals in the year, no month given
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME HERE IS `carpenter`, one of the fifty the Newberry index (T-0570) flagged against this work. An arrival YEAR for eight men, seven of whom the project already holds under some spelling, and all of whom are in the town before the scene date of 1835-07-01. It is a year and not a date: the sentence gives no month, and a run wanting Carpenter's month must go to bk_mose1_013, which fixes it within a month of 19 August 1832. This volume is 1895 and sixty years after the fact; it is a compiler and not a witness, and nothing here may be graded above the ladder's reading for a retrospective secondary work.

claims.notes: THE MOST PLACEABLE SENTENCE IN THIS READING, and it names no lead surname. A building with a MATERIAL (log), a STOREY COUNT (story-and-a-half), a FOOTPRINT (45x18) and a POSITION (the angle where Lake and South Water meet) — four of the five fields data/structures/ wants, and the fifth, the orientation, is implied by the angle and not stated. Whether the town of 1835-07-01 still had it there is NOT said here: the arrangement is described from November 1832 and the same volume (page 89 of this chapter and the postmaster list at page 545 and following) has Hogan in the office until 3 March 1837, which is a reason to look and not a licence to assume. claims.normalized: The State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 showed the population of Chicago at 3,297, and counted forty-four stores (dry goods, hardware and groceries), two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. Nine of the buildings erected were of brick.
claims.describes_date: the count was taken between 1 September and December 1835 — TWO TO FIVE MONTHS AFTER the scene date of 1835-07-01
claims.notes: THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL PARAGRAPH IN THE VOLUME FOR THIS PROJECT, and it dates itself out of the scene by two to five months. It is a TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN: not who kept a store, but how many stores there were, and the same for druggists, taverns, printing offices, lawyers and physicians. The project has never held a denominator for its business layer, and this is one — for December 1835 and not for July, which is the whole of the caution. THE POPULATION FIGURE IS ALREADY IN THE REPOSITORY from two other routes: the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-01 and the Chicago American of 1835-06-08 and 1835-06-27 carry 3,297 in data/research/newspapers/, so this is a third printing of a number the project holds, not a new one. THE TRADE COUNTS ARE NOT: no file under data/ carries "forty-four stores" or its numeral before this reading. What it does NOT give is a single name, a single address, or the enumerator's own schedule — it is a summary of a count this project does not hold, at one remove, sixty years later.

claims.normalized: Peck's little log store stood close to Fort Dearborn but was only a temporary location. He then built a two-storey frame structure — the first in the village — on what was, in 1895, the south-east corner of La Salle and South Water streets. The lumber, sawn from black walnut trees, was brought from Detroit by boat; mechanics and building material were almost unobtainable and the building took some time to complete, but it was occupied and the goods moved into it from the log store in the fall of 1831.
claims.describes_date: the log store before it, and the frame store occupied in the fall of 1831
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `peck`, and this is the most detailed building description the volume gives of a private commercial structure in the town: TWO STOREYS, FRAME, black walnut lumber shipped from Detroit, on the SOUTH-EAST CORNER of La Salle and South Water, occupied in the fall of 1831 and therefore standing on the scene date unless something took it down. It also records the log store that preceded it, "close to Fort Dearborn", with no closer position than that. IT DISAGREES WITH PAGE 89 OF THE SAME BOOK about which building was first — page 89 (bk_mose1_002) calls Dole's and Peck's the first frame buildings used for business purposes and dates the pair to 1832; this page calls Peck's the first two-storey frame structure in the village and dates it to 1831. Both readings are recorded; neither is adopted, and the reconciliation belongs to data/structures/ under the ladder, in that layer's own PR. "What is now" is 1895 street naming applied to 1831 ground.

It bears on the household two ways and settles neither: Caton was ABSENT from Chicago for the journey and the wedding, and he came back with a wife, which is a household of two where the project may hold one. claims.normalized: Within a month after his arrival, on 19 August 1832, Philo Carpenter organised a Sunday school — one of the first in Chicago — of thirteen children and five adults.
claims.describes_date: 19 August 1832, and by implication an arrival within the month before it

claims.notes: TWO THINGS, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE TO USE. First, this is the RULE OF A ROSTER the project does not hold: a list of every person known to have had a residence at Chicago before 1830, with NATIVITY, YEAR and REMARKS columns, running from "Ament, Edward G." across pages 78 and 79 — about thirty rows, giving for each a nativity, a year of arrival and a note of taxes paid in 1825 or votes cast in 1826, 1828 or 1830. That roster is NOT transcribed here: it is a records-shaped dataset and a reading of it is its own unit of work, filed as a ticket by this run rather than half-done inside a claims file. Second, and independent of it, the footnote states in its own words WHY Hubbard is absent — he did not take up a permanent residence until 1832 — which is a dated statement about permanent residence for a man this project holds, made by a compiler who had to decide the question in order to build his list. It is not a witness and it is 1895; it is a reason, and reasons are what the ladder grades. The list credits Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 three lines above it, and this project HOLDS Hurlbut at data/research/books/text/hurlbut_chicago_antiquities_28_36.txt — pages 28 to 36, which stop one page short of the cited run.

claims.notes: THE ONLY SENTENCE IN THIS READING THAT DESCRIBES THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, and it is the closest one in time: the winter that ended four or five months before 1835-07-01. It says three separable things — little snow, doors open all winter, and cattle grazing living grass on the river bank — and the third is the one a reconstruction can use, because it is a statement about the state of the bank vegetation through a winter, not about the weather. IT IS EVIDENCE FOR THE PRECEDING WINTER AND NOT FOR JULY, and it must never be cited for the scene's own ground cover. THE CHAIN IS LONG AND IS STATED: a diarist's private memoranda, gathered into a fifty-year retrospect by the same hand, deposited at the Chicago Historical Society, and printed here in 1895 by a compiler who names neither the diarist in this line nor the date the notes were written. The claim is graded transcription_mediated like every other in this file, and the length of that chain is a reason to weigh it lightly, not a reason to leave it unrecorded.

"What is now Monroe street" is 1895 naming laid over 1834 prairie, and the elm is gone; the passage says the market was on the prairie, which in the winter of 1833-4 was OUTSIDE the platted town, and a run that places it inside the block grid will have invented the thing the sentence is carefully not saying. entities: the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company

claims.notes: FOUR LEAD SURNAMES IN ONE ROLL — `peck`, `hubbard`, `lathrop` and `hyde` — and twenty-two named men who were in the town in the autumn of 1835. It is the largest single list of townsmen in this reading, and it is a PRESENCE list and nothing more: signing a fire company roll says a man was there and says nothing about his trade, his household or where he lived. IT IS THREE MONTHS PAST THE SCENE DATE. A man on this roll was in Chicago on 7 October 1835; whether he was there on 1 July is a separate question for every one of the twenty-two, and the volume does not answer it. THE VOLUME CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON THE DATE: this page has the company formed on 7 October 1835 at the trustees' meeting, while page 570's biography of Peck (bk_mose1_010's neighbour, quoted at bk_mose1_009) has the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company "organized October 20th, 1835". Both are recorded; neither is adopted; a fortnight is exactly the kind of gap a compiler working from two sources leaves behind. The purchase list is also a small inventory of the town's entire firefighting equipment at that date, bought for $29.63.
